list.listitem: The diagnosis of patellofemoral pain syndrome is clinical and centered around a combination of key historical and physical exam findings. B
The mainstay of treatment includes education as well as a dedicated physical therapy program. Physical therapy exercises include hip and knee strengthening and valgus control exercises. A
A short course of NSAIDS for initial pain control can also be considered. B

background.definition: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (also called "runner's knee") is characterized by diffuse peripatellar or retropatellar pain in the absence of intraarticular findings and is often associated with activities that load the patellofemoral joint such as descending or ascending stairs, squatting, prolonged sitting, running, and cycling.

list.listitem: Patellofemoral pain syndrome accounts for 25% of all knee injuries treated in sports medicine clinics.
Patellofemoral knee pain can account for almost 10% of all visits and 20% to 40% of all knee problems in clinics that manage musculoskeletal problems.
It is the most common knee problem encountered by primary care providers in the outpatient setting.

A large Dutch primary care study found an incidence of 3.4/1000 person-years in children and young adults (7 to 24 years). The incidence was twice as high in girls than boys (4.6 vs 2.4 per 1000 person-years) and peaked at age 13.
Anatomic conditions that are thought to predispose patients to patellofemoral syndrome are listed under "Risk Factors."
It is largely a condition caused and mediated by biomechanical forces.
Leg length discrepancies, muscle imbalance, and differing activity levels have shown consistent statistical association with patellofemoral pain.

Overuse or training errors, abnormal patellar tracking, acute trauma (eg, a lateral blow to the patella with the knee flexed), and a gait change secondary concurrent lower extremity injury are also the possible causes.

Seven key factors have been proposed to contribute to and help define patellofemoral pain syndrome: Vastus medialis obliquus deficiency, medial patellofemoral ligament laxity, lateral retinaculum tightness, increased quadriceps angle, hip abductor weakness, patella alta, and trochlear dysplasia.
The patella facilitates knee extension, distributes the forces of the quadriceps evenly by acting as a lever, and protects the patellar tendon from friction.
Changes in patellar tilt, rotation, or medial-lateral position as the knee goes through a range of motion may alter the distribution of forces and result in pain.

The structures that contain nerve fibers capable of transmitting pain, and hence the most likely pain generators in patellofemoral pain syndrome, are the anterior synovium, the infrapatellar fat pad, the subchondral bone, the patellar or quadriceps tendons, and the lateral or medial retinaculae.
The diagnosis of patellofemoral pain syndrome is clinical and based on a consistent history with a corroborating physical exam. B
The physical exam findings that appear to best rule in the diagnosis when present are Q angle >20°, abnormal active instability test, retinacular tenderness, and patellofemoral joint crepitations. C
Radiographs are not routinely required for the diagnosis of patellofemoral pain, but may be considered in select cases. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Mechanical symptoms; more likely to have an effusion and/or a history of trauma
An intraoperative or MRI finding of softening or fibrillation of the retropatellar cartilage
Tenderness laterally over the femoral epicondyle; may demonstrate a positive Ober test
Tenderness over the insertion of the patellar tendon at the tibial tubercle
Maximal tenderness to palpation over the involved tendons
Tenderness and swelling over antermedial tibia (pes bursa) or the patella (prepatellar bursa)
Tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella at the insertion of the patellar tendon
Tenderness directly over patella with appropriate radiographic finding
Tenderness over the infrapatellar fat pad
Tenderness usually over the plica (redundant synovium fold) just medial to the patella

list.listitem: The typical patient presents with anterior knee pain that is worse with descending stairs or when seated with the knees flexed for a prolonged time (theater sign). Activities that are weight bearing with the knee flexed tend to worsen symptoms.

Other common historical findings include knee stiffness, the sensation of the knee giving out due to sharp pain, the sensation of crepitus or popping in the knee, and a notable change in the frequency, duration, or intensity of physical activity.
Swelling and locking are not common features of patellofemoral pain syndrome.

A small, poor quality study assessed the accuracy of key physical examination maneuvers. The study compared patients with clinically diagnosed patellofemoral pain with healthy controls without knee pain, which if anything will inflate the accuracy of these maneuvers.
An abnormal patellar tilt tests (LR+ 5.4) is moderately useful in ruling in the condition.

The researchers found that a Q angle >20°, retinacular sensitvity, patellofemoral join crepitations, and an abnormal 'active instability test' were best at ruling in patellofemoral pain syndrome. Only absence of lateral retinacular sensitivity was good at ruling out the condition.
Absence of pain during squatting is helpful to rule out patellofemoral syndrome, one meta-analysis shows a negative likelihood ratio 0.2.
Radiographs are not routinely recommended as a part of the initial evaluation of patellofemoral pain.
There is currently limited evidence for the use of ultrasound in the diagnosis of patellofemoral pain syndrome.

A study of 61 male infantry soldiers with patellofemoral pain syndrome and 25 control subjects showed that patellar subluxation was the only radiographic finding different between the soldiers with patellofemoral pain syndrome and the control subjects.

Imaging (plain films and/or MRI) may be considered if there is a history of trauma or surgery, if there is an effusion, if the patient is not improving, if a bipartite patella is suspected, if the patient is older than 50 years, or if the patient is skeletally immature (see ).
See for a suggested approach to the evaluation of patients with anterior knee pain.

Physical therapy, especially eccentric quad training, should be considered for strengthening and flexibility of the quadriceps and hip abductors and for correction of other identified deficiencies noted on physical exam. B
A short course of NSAIDS may be useful for initial, but not long-term, pain reduction. B
A Cochrane review of four trials found that there is limited evidence for the effectiveness of the use of NSAIDS for short-term pain relief in patellofemoral pain.

The abovementioned review also found two contradictory trials regarding glycosaminoglycan polysulphate injections for patellofemoral pain syndrome and recommended further study of this form of treatment.

The review identified one trial reporting limited evidence for injectable nandrolone (an anabolic steroid), but notes that the use of this drug is highly controversial and is therefore not recommended outside of clinical trials.
Surgery: There is no good evidence to support surgical treatment for patellofemoral pain syndrome unless another cause of knee pain is discovered during diagnostic workup that may warrant surgery.,

Regenerative medicine/Orthobiologics: There is some evidence for agents such as platelet-rich plasma and mesenchymal stem cells for conditions that can masquerade as patellofemoral pain syndrome, such as patellofemoral arthritis, but as patellofemoral pain syndrome is a biomechanical process these therapies are not indicated.
Corticosteroid injections: There is very little evidence to support use of corticosteroid injections in the management of patellofemoral pain syndrome.

Pulsed signal therapy was found to be effective at 3 months in a small double-blinded sham controlled randomized trial of 25 patients / 41 knees age 20 to 50 with isolated patellofemoral pain syndrome.

The 2018 Consensus statement from the British Journal of Sports Medicine on treatment modalities for patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) endorses more evidence-based approaches to treatment which include the use of exercise therapy (especially the combination of hip-focused and knee-focused exercises), combined interventions and foot orthoses to improve pain and/or function.

A Cochrane review of 12 trials found limited evidence that exercise physical therapy is more effective than no exercise in reducing patellofemoral pain. The review also found that both open and closed chain kinetic exercises were equally effective at reducing patellofemoral pain.
Closed chain exercises include those that involve contact of the foot with a surface such as leg presses and squats.
Open chain exercises include those that involve no contact of the foot with a surface such as leg raises, leg extensions, and leg curls.

A study of female collegiate athletes with patellofemoral pain showed that a 6-week rehabilitation focusing on strengthening the affected hip abductors led to return to pain-free running in 22 of 24 runners with patellofemoral pain.
Foot exercises, foot orthoses, and knee exercise provides greater relief at 4 months but not much benefit at 12 months.

A trial of 136 patients assigned to a home exercise program, patellar bracing, a home exercise program with patellar bracing, or a home exercise program with a knee sleeve found that symptoms of patellofemoral pain syndrome improved regardless of the treatment group. Patellar bracing did not improve symptoms more quickly when added to a home program, but if used alone was effective at improving symptoms of patellofemoral pain syndrome.
A systematic review found that there was a dose-response relationship between more frequent exercise and less pain.
There is insufficient evidence to support patellar taping.
Gait retraining from a rearview strike to forefoot strike decreases pain without changing running economy.
Low load blood flow restriction has a greater reduction in pain with daily living at 8 weeks.
One study showed that exercises in addition to education provided no additional long term benefit so education on symptoms and management should be a part of the mainstay of treatment.

If greater lateral core endurance, less anterior core endurance, patients tend to do better with hip and core strengthening. If patients are at a decreased weight, have weaker hip internal rotation, stronger hip external rotation, greater trunch extension endurance, they do better with knee strengthening.

A randomized trial compared standard physiotherapy with physiotherapy + core postural control training in women with PFPS and found greater pain reduction and function production with the addition of core training.
Valgus control instruction exercises improves performance and can be used to improve strength, decrease pain, and decrease injury.
A knee brace for 2 weeks may help patients feel more confident in knee function.
Medially directed realignment brace can provide short term pain relief over exercise alone after 6 and 12 weeks.
A brief psychological intervention can help improve symptoms in adolescents in the short term.

A study on the use of ultrasound combined with ice massage contrast (3 minutes of heat application followed by 2 minutes of ice massage) showed that there was a trend toward a greater pain reduction and strength increase with the active ultrasound group, but the trend did not reach statistical significance.
Patterned electrical neuromuscular stimulation (PENS) can provide pain relief at 6 and 12 months.
Long-term prognosis appears good, and in most cases, patellofemoral pain syndrome does not result in chronic disability or radiographic abnormalities. B
Although pain may become chronic and limit a patient from physical activities, in most patients patellofemoral pain syndrome does not lead to patellofemoral osteoarthritis. C

algorithm.title: Suggested Approach to the Patient with Anterior Knee Pain.

cell.label: Patient with anterior knee pain. Perform directed history and physical. Other causes of knee pain more likely?
Patient: - over 50? - skeletally immature? - h/o trauma or surgery? - effusion? - failing conservative treatment? - suspected bipartite patella?
Diagnose and treat patellofemoral pain syndrome.
Further evaluation and treatment for other causes of knee pain.
